What is assembly language and what is the relationship between assembly and machine code?

Assembly language is a low-level programming language with a strong correspondence to machine code instructions. Each line of assembly maps to one (or very few) CPU instructions.

Key characteristics:
- Assembly is human-readable; machine code is binary
- Each assembly mnemonic (like `mov`, `add`, `jmp`) maps directly to a CPU opcode
- There is almost no abstraction — you control registers, memory, and flags directly

This reference covers **x86-64 (AMD64)** assembly using **NASM syntax**.

What are the main x86-64 assemblers?

- **NASM** (Netwide Assembler) — cross-platform, popular for Linux, uses Intel syntax
- **MASM** (Microsoft Macro Assembler) — Windows, Intel syntax
- **GAS** (GNU Assembler) — part of binutils, uses AT&T syntax by default, used by `gcc`
- **FASM** (Flat Assembler) — self-hosting, very fast

Write a Hello World program in x86-64 assembly for Linux using NASM.

```nasm
; hello.asm — x86-64 Linux
section .data
    msg db "Hello, World!", 10   ; message + newline (10 = '\n')
    len equ $ - msg              ; length = current position minus start of msg

section .text
    global _start

_start:
    ; sys_write(stdout, msg, len)
    mov rax, 1          ; syscall number: write
    mov rdi, 1          ; file descriptor: stdout
    mov rsi, msg        ; pointer to buffer
    mov rdx, len        ; number of bytes to write
    syscall

    ; sys_exit(0)
    mov rax, 60         ; syscall number: exit
    xor rdi, rdi        ; exit code 0 (xor is faster than mov rdi,0)
    syscall
```

Assemble and run:
```bash
nasm -f elf64 hello.asm -o hello.o
ld hello.o -o hello
./hello
```

How do you assemble and link a NASM program on Linux?

```bash
# Assemble to object file
nasm -f elf64 hello.asm -o hello.o

# Link to executable (no C runtime)
ld hello.o -o hello

./hello

# Alternative: link with C runtime (macOS/Windows friendly)
nasm -f elf64 hello.asm
gcc hello.o -o hello -nostartfiles
```

- `-f elf64` specifies the 64-bit ELF output format (Linux)
- `ld` is the GNU linker, used when you write your own `_start` entry point
- `-nostartfiles` skips the C startup code but uses the C linker

What are the x86-64 general-purpose registers and their sub-registers?

Each register has four sizes you can access independently:

```
; 64-bit registers
rax  rcx  rdx  rbx  rsp  rbp  rsi  rdi
r8   r9   r10  r11  r12  r13  r14  r15

; 32-bit sub-registers (writing zero-extends to 64-bit)
eax  ecx  edx  ebx  esp  ebp  esi  edi
r8d  r9d  r10d r11d r12d r13d r14d r15d

; 16-bit sub-registers
ax   cx   dx   bx   sp   bp   si   di
r8w  r9w  r10w r11w r12w r13w r14w r15w

; 8-bit sub-registers (low byte)
al   cl   dl   bl   spl  bpl  sil  dil
r8b  r9b  r10b r11b r12b r13b r14b r15b

; 8-bit high bytes (only ax,cx,dx,bx)
ah   ch   dh   bh
```

Important: writing to a 32-bit register (e.g., `eax`) **zero-extends** the result into the full 64-bit `rax`. Writing to 8-bit or 16-bit sub-registers does **not** zero-extend.

What are the special-purpose registers in x86-64?

```
rip     ; instruction pointer — address of next instruction to execute
rsp     ; stack pointer — top of the stack (grows downward)
rbp     ; base pointer / frame pointer — tracks the current stack frame
rflags  ; flags register — holds ZF, SF, OF, CF, PF etc.

; Segment registers (mostly legacy in 64-bit mode)
cs  ds  es  fs  gs  ss

; SIMD registers
xmm0..xmm15    ; 128-bit (SSE/SSE2)
ymm0..ymm15    ; 256-bit (AVX)
zmm0..zmm31    ; 512-bit (AVX-512)
```

`rip` cannot be moved to directly — it is controlled by `jmp`, `call`, and `ret`.

What is the Linux System V AMD64 calling convention?

The **System V AMD64** calling convention is used on Linux, macOS, and BSDs:

```
; Function arguments (in order):
rdi  rsi  rdx  rcx  r8  r9   ; first 6 integer/pointer args
; additional args go on the stack

; Return values:
rax       ; first return value (or only)
rdx       ; second return value (e.g. for 128-bit results)

; Callee-saved (function must preserve these):
rbx  rbp  r12  r13  r14  r15

; Caller-saved (may be clobbered by any call):
rax  rcx  rdx  rsi  rdi  r8  r9  r10  r11
```

If your function uses any callee-saved register, it must push it at the start and pop it before returning.

What is the Windows x64 calling convention?

The **Windows x64** calling convention differs from Linux:

```
; Function arguments (in order):
rcx  rdx  r8  r9   ; first 4 integer/pointer args
; additional args go on the stack
; caller must also allocate 32 bytes of "shadow space" on the stack before each call

; Return value:
rax

; Callee-saved (function must preserve these):
rbx  rbp  rdi  rsi  r12  r13  r14  r15
; also: xmm6..xmm15

; Caller-saved (may be clobbered):
rax  rcx  rdx  r8  r9  r10  r11
```

Key difference from Linux: Windows uses `rcx rdx r8 r9` (not `rdi rsi rdx rcx`), and requires 32 bytes of shadow space on the stack before every call.

How do you define data in the .data and .bss sections in NASM?

```nasm
section .data
    byte_val  db 42          ; define byte  (1 byte)
    word_val  dw 1000        ; define word  (2 bytes)
    dword_val dd 100000      ; define dword (4 bytes)
    qword_val dq 1000000000  ; define qword (8 bytes)
    my_array  dd 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
    my_str    db "Hello", 0  ; null-terminated string

section .bss
    buffer  resb 256         ; reserve 256 bytes (uninitialized)
    count   resq 1           ; reserve 1 qword (8 bytes)
```

- `.data` — initialized data (takes space in the binary)
- `.bss` — uninitialized data (zero-filled at runtime, no space in binary)
- `db/dw/dd/dq` — define byte/word/dword/qword
- `resb/resw/resd/resq` — reserve bytes/words/dwords/qwords

How does the MOV instruction work in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
; Register to register
mov rax, 42
mov rbx, rax

; Immediate to register
mov rax, 100             ; 64-bit immediate
mov eax, 100             ; 32-bit (zero-extends to rax)
mov ax,  100             ; 16-bit
mov al,  100             ; 8-bit

; Memory to register
mov rax, [qword_val]     ; load qword from memory
mov eax, [dword_val]
mov ax,  [word_val]
mov al,  [byte_val]

; Register to memory
mov [qword_val], rax
mov qword [buffer], 0    ; explicit size override
```

Note: `mov` cannot move directly from memory to memory — you always need a register as an intermediate.

How does memory addressing work in x86-64? Show the effective address formula.

x86-64 supports a flexible addressing mode:
```
[base + index*scale + displacement]
```

```nasm
mov rax, [rsi]              ; base only
mov rax, [rsi + 8]          ; base + displacement
mov rax, [rsi + rcx*8]      ; base + index*scale (scale: 1,2,4,8)
mov rax, [rsi + rcx*4 + 16] ; base + index*scale + displacement

mov rax, [my_array + 4]     ; element at byte offset 4
```

- **base**: any general-purpose register
- **index**: any register except `rsp`
- **scale**: 1, 2, 4, or 8 (byte multiplier)
- **displacement**: signed constant offset

What is LEA and how is it different from MOV?

```nasm
; MOV loads the VALUE at the address
mov rax, [rsi + rcx*8]   ; rax = *(rsi + rcx*8)

; LEA computes the ADDRESS without accessing memory
lea rax, [rsi + rcx*8]   ; rax = rsi + rcx*8  (just arithmetic, no load)
lea rdi, [my_str]         ; rdi = address of my_str (like &my_str in C)
```

LEA (Load Effective Address) is often used as a fast arithmetic trick:
```nasm
lea rax, [rax + rax*4]   ; rax = rax * 5  (1 instruction, no multiply)
lea rax, [rax*2 + rax]   ; rax = rax * 3
```

What are MOVZX and MOVSX used for?

```nasm
; MOVZX — move with zero-extension
movzx rax, byte [buffer]    ; load byte, zero-extend to 64-bit rax
movzx eax, word [word_val]  ; load word, zero-extend to 32-bit eax

; MOVSX — move with sign-extension
movsx rax, dword [dword_val] ; load dword, sign-extend to 64-bit rax
movsx rax, byte [buffer]     ; load signed byte, sign-extend to 64-bit
```

- **MOVZX**: fills the upper bits with **zeros** — treats the source as an unsigned value
- **MOVSX**: fills the upper bits with the **sign bit** — treats the source as a signed (two's complement) value

Without these, moving a smaller value into a larger register leaves the upper bits undefined (or unchanged).

How do XCHG, PUSH, POP, and CMOV work?

```nasm
; XCHG — swap two registers atomically
xchg rax, rbx              ; rax ↔ rbx

; PUSH — push value onto stack (rsp -= 8, then store)
push rax
push rbx

; POP — pop value from stack (load, then rsp += 8)
pop  rcx     ; rcx = old rbx (LIFO order)
pop  rdx     ; rdx = old rax

; CMOV — conditional move (no branch!)
cmp rax, rbx
cmovg rax, rbx   ; move rbx→rax only if rax > rbx (greater)
cmovl rax, rbx   ; move rbx→rax only if rax < rbx (less)
```

`cmov` variants avoid branch mispredictions — useful for simple if/else patterns on modern CPUs.

How do ADD, SUB, INC, and DEC work in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
; ADD — addition
add rax, rbx       ; rax = rax + rbx
add rax, 10        ; rax = rax + 10  (immediate)
add rax, [mem]     ; rax = rax + value at mem

; SUB — subtraction
sub rax, rbx       ; rax = rax - rbx
sub rax, [mem]

; INC — increment by 1
inc rax             ; rax++

; DEC — decrement by 1
dec rcx             ; rcx--
```

All of these set the flags (ZF, SF, OF, CF) based on the result, which can then be used for conditional jumps.

How does multiplication work in x86-64 assembly (MUL and IMUL)?

```nasm
; MUL — unsigned multiply
; rdx:rax = rax * operand  (128-bit result in two registers)
mul rbx            ; rdx:rax = rax * rbx

; IMUL — signed multiply (three forms)
imul rbx           ; rdx:rax = rax * rbx  (1 operand, like MUL but signed)
imul rax, rbx      ; rax = rax * rbx      (2 operand, result truncated to 64-bit)
imul rax, rbx, 5   ; rax = rbx * 5        (3 operand, immediate)
```

- 1-operand MUL/IMUL always uses `rax` as one input and stores the 128-bit result across `rdx:rax`
- 2-operand and 3-operand IMUL are more convenient and keep the result in one register (overflow is silently truncated)

How does division work in x86-64 assembly (DIV and IDIV)?

```nasm
; DIV — unsigned divide
; rdx:rax ÷ operand → rax = quotient, rdx = remainder
xor rdx, rdx       ; MUST clear rdx before dividing (set upper 64 bits to 0)
mov rax, 100
mov rbx, 7
div rbx            ; rax = 14 (quotient), rdx = 2 (remainder)

; IDIV — signed divide (same register convention)
cdq                ; sign-extend rax into rdx:rax (for signed division)
idiv rbx
```

**Important**: always clear (or sign-extend) `rdx` before dividing, or you will get wrong results or a divide exception. Use `xor rdx, rdx` for unsigned, `cqo` (or `cdq`) for signed.

How do bitwise operations work in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
; AND
and rax, rbx
and rax, 0xFF      ; mask: keep only lowest 8 bits

; OR
or  rax, rbx
or  rax, 0x01      ; set bit 0

; XOR
xor rax, rax       ; rax = 0  (fastest way to zero a register)
xor rax, 0xFF      ; flip lowest 8 bits

; NOT
not rax            ; bitwise NOT (flip all bits)

; NEG
neg rax            ; rax = -rax  (two's complement negate)
```

How do shift and rotate instructions work in x86-64?

```nasm
; SHL — shift left (multiply by 2 per shift)
shl rax, 1         ; rax = rax * 2
shl rax, cl        ; shift left by amount in cl register

; SHR — logical shift right (unsigned division by 2 per shift)
shr rax, 1         ; rax = rax / 2  (unsigned)

; SAR — arithmetic shift right (signed, preserves sign bit)
sar rax, 1         ; rax = rax / 2  (signed, sign-extends)

; ROL / ROR — rotate left / rotate right (bits wrap around)
rol rax, 4         ; rotate left by 4 bits
ror rax, 4         ; rotate right by 4 bits
```

- SHR fills the high bits with **0** (unsigned)
- SAR fills the high bits with the **sign bit** (signed)
- Rotate does not lose bits — they wrap to the other end

How do BSF, BSR, and POPCNT work?

```nasm
; BSF — Bit Scan Forward: find index of lowest set bit
bsf rcx, rax       ; rcx = position of lowest 1-bit in rax
                   ; ZF=1 if rax=0 (undefined result)

; BSR — Bit Scan Reverse: find index of highest set bit
bsr rcx, rax       ; rcx = position of highest 1-bit in rax

; POPCNT — population count: count the number of set bits
popcnt rax, rbx    ; rax = number of 1-bits in rbx
```

Example: if `rax = 0b00101000` (40):
- `bsf` → 3 (lowest set bit is bit 3)
- `bsr` → 5 (highest set bit is bit 5)
- `popcnt` → 2 (two 1-bits)

What are the CPU flags and what do they represent?

Arithmetic and logical instructions set flags in the `rflags` register:

```
ZF — Zero Flag:     set if result == 0
SF — Sign Flag:     set if result < 0 (MSB is 1)
OF — Overflow Flag: set if signed overflow occurred
CF — Carry Flag:    set if unsigned overflow / borrow occurred
PF — Parity Flag:   set if low byte has even number of 1-bits
```

These flags are then read by conditional jump instructions:
- `je` (jump if equal) checks ZF
- `jg` (jump if greater) checks ZF=0 and SF=OF
- `jb` (jump if below) checks CF=1

Flags are set by: `add`, `sub`, `cmp`, `test`, `and`, `or`, `xor`, etc.

How do CMP and TEST work? How are they different?

```nasm
; CMP — compare by subtraction (sets flags, discards result)
cmp rax, rbx      ; computes rax - rbx, updates flags, does NOT change rax or rbx
cmp rax, 0        ; check if rax == 0

; TEST — compare by AND (sets flags, discards result)
test rax, rax     ; computes rax & rax — sets ZF if rax == 0
test al, 1        ; checks if bit 0 of al is set (ZF=0 means bit is set)
```

- `cmp a, b` is best for comparing two values (equal, greater, less)
- `test a, a` is the idiomatic way to check if a register is zero
- `test a, mask` checks whether specific bits are set

Neither instruction modifies their operands — they only affect flags.

What are the conditional jump instructions in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
; Unconditional
jmp label          ; always jump
jmp rax            ; indirect jump (jump to address in rax)

; Signed comparisons (use after cmp with signed integers)
je  label  ; jump if equal          (ZF=1)
jne label  ; jump if not equal      (ZF=0)
jg  label  ; jump if greater        (ZF=0 and SF=OF)
jge label  ; jump if greater/equal  (SF=OF)
jl  label  ; jump if less           (SF≠OF)
jle label  ; jump if less/equal     (ZF=1 or SF≠OF)

; Unsigned comparisons (use after cmp with unsigned integers)
ja  label  ; jump if above          (CF=0 and ZF=0)
jae label  ; jump if above/equal    (CF=0)
jb  label  ; jump if below          (CF=1)
jbe label  ; jump if below/equal    (CF=1 or ZF=1)

; Flag-based
jz  label  ; jump if zero  (ZF=1)
jnz label  ; jump if not zero
jc  label  ; jump if carry
jnc label  ; jump if no carry
js  label  ; jump if sign (result was negative)
jns label  ; jump if no sign (result was non-negative)
jo  label  ; jump if overflow
jno label  ; jump if no overflow
```

How do you implement a loop in x86-64 assembly? Show the LOOP instruction and a manual loop.

```nasm
; Using the LOOP instruction (decrements rcx, jumps if rcx != 0)
mov rcx, 10
.loop:
    ; loop body here
    loop .loop        ; rcx--; if rcx != 0: jump to .loop

; Manual loop (more flexible, preferred in modern code)
mov rcx, 10
.loop:
    ; loop body here
    dec rcx
    jnz .loop         ; jump if rcx != 0

; Counting up
xor rax, rax          ; rax = 0 (loop counter)
.loop:
    ; use rax
    inc rax
    cmp rax, 10
    jl  .loop         ; jump if rax < 10
```

The `loop` instruction is convenient but slower on modern CPUs — a `dec`/`jnz` pair is preferred for performance.

How do CALL and RET work in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
; CALL — push return address, jump to function
call my_function   ; pushes rip+next_instruction, then jumps to my_function
; execution resumes here after ret

; RET — pop return address and jump to it
my_function:
    ; function body
    ret              ; pops the address pushed by call, jumps there
```

`call label` is equivalent to:
```nasm
push rip + 5        ; (address of next instruction)
jmp  label
```

`ret` is equivalent to:
```nasm
pop rip             ; restore instruction pointer
```

The stack must be 16-byte aligned before a `call` (required by System V ABI).

How do you pass arguments to a function in x86-64 assembly (System V)?

```nasm
; System V AMD64: arguments go in registers (in order)
mov rdi, arg1      ; 1st argument
mov rsi, arg2      ; 2nd argument
mov rdx, arg3      ; 3rd argument
mov rcx, arg4      ; 4th argument
mov r8,  arg5      ; 5th argument
mov r9,  arg6      ; 6th argument
; 7th+ arguments go on the stack (right to left)
call my_func
; return value is in rax
```

Inside the function:
```nasm
my_func:
    ; rdi = first arg, rsi = second arg, etc.
    mov rax, rdi     ; return the first argument
    ret
```

What is the standard function prologue and epilogue in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
my_function:
    ; --- Prologue ---
    push rbp            ; save caller's base pointer
    mov  rbp, rsp       ; set our frame pointer
    sub  rsp, 48        ; allocate local stack space (keep 16-byte aligned)

    ; Save any callee-saved registers we will use
    push rbx
    push r12
    push r13

    ; --- Function body ---
    ; Parameters in: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9
    ; Return value:  rax

    ; --- Epilogue ---
    pop r13
    pop r12
    pop rbx

    mov rsp, rbp        ; restore stack pointer
    pop rbp             ; restore caller's base pointer
    ret
```

The stack must remain **16-byte aligned** at every `call` instruction. The `push rbp` + `sub rsp, N` pattern ensures this when N is chosen carefully.

Write a recursive factorial function in x86-64 assembly.

```nasm
; factorial(n) — n passed in rdi, result returned in rax
factorial:
    push rbp
    mov  rbp, rsp
    push rbx
    mov  rbx, rdi       ; save n (we need it after the recursive call)

    cmp  rdi, 1
    jle  .base_case     ; if n <= 1, return 1

    dec  rdi            ; n - 1
    call factorial       ; rax = factorial(n-1)
    imul rax, rbx        ; rax = n * factorial(n-1)
    jmp  .done

.base_case:
    mov  rax, 1         ; return 1

.done:
    pop  rbx
    pop  rbp
    ret
```

Key points:
- `rbx` is callee-saved, so it is safe to use for storing `n` across the recursive call
- `rdi` is caller-saved and will be clobbered by the recursive call — that is why we save `n` in `rbx`

What is the difference between callee-saved and caller-saved registers?

**Caller-saved** (volatile) registers: the calling function must save them before a call if it needs them afterward — the called function may freely overwrite them.
```
rax  rcx  rdx  rsi  rdi  r8  r9  r10  r11
```

**Callee-saved** (non-volatile) registers: the called function must save and restore them if it uses them — the caller can rely on them being unchanged after a call.
```
rbx  rbp  r12  r13  r14  r15
```

Example: if you call a function and need `rcx` afterward, save it before the call:
```nasm
push rcx         ; save caller-saved register
call some_func
pop  rcx         ; restore it
```

How do SSE2 SIMD operations work in x86-64 assembly?

SSE2 operates on 128-bit `xmm` registers holding multiple values simultaneously:

```nasm
section .data
    floats  dd 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0   ; 4 packed single-precision floats

section .text
    ; Load 4 floats into xmm0
    movaps  xmm0, [floats]   ; aligned load (address must be 16-byte aligned)
    movups  xmm0, [floats]   ; unaligned load (no alignment requirement)

    ; Packed single-precision arithmetic (4 floats at once)
    addps   xmm0, xmm1       ; xmm0[0..3] += xmm1[0..3]
    subps   xmm0, xmm1
    mulps   xmm0, xmm1
    divps   xmm0, xmm1
    sqrtps  xmm0, xmm1       ; square root of all 4 floats

    ; Scalar (operates on only the lowest element)
    addss   xmm0, xmm1       ; xmm0[0] += xmm1[0], others unchanged
    mulss   xmm0, xmm1

    ; Double precision
    addpd   xmm0, xmm1       ; 2 doubles added
    addsd   xmm0, xmm1       ; 1 double added (scalar)
```

`ps` = packed single | `pd` = packed double | `ss` = scalar single | `sd` = scalar double

How do SSE compare and shuffle instructions work?

```nasm
; Compare — element-wise, sets each element to all-1s (true) or 0 (false)
cmpeqps xmm0, xmm1       ; xmm0[i] = (xmm0[i] == xmm1[i]) ? 0xFFFFFFFF : 0

; Shuffle / permute — rearrange elements within xmm registers
shufps  xmm0, xmm1, 0b01001110
; Immediate byte encodes which elements from xmm0 and xmm1 go where
; bits [1:0] → dest[0], bits [3:2] → dest[1] (from xmm0)
; bits [5:4] → dest[2], bits [7:6] → dest[3] (from xmm1)
```

SSE comparisons produce a **mask** (all 1s or all 0s per element) that can then be used with `andps`/`orps` to blend values.

How do AVX 256-bit SIMD operations work?

AVX uses 256-bit `ymm` registers (8 floats or 4 doubles at once):

```nasm
; Load 8 floats into ymm0
vmovaps  ymm0, [floats8]     ; aligned 256-bit load

; 3-operand arithmetic (non-destructive, result goes to dest)
vaddps   ymm0, ymm0, ymm1   ; ymm0 = ymm0 + ymm1  (8 floats)
vmulps   ymm2, ymm0, ymm1   ; ymm2 = ymm0 * ymm1  (ymm0 unchanged)
```

AVX uses a 3-operand form: `vOPps dest, src1, src2` — unlike SSE's 2-operand destructive form `addps xmm0, xmm1` which always overwrites the first operand.

AVX-512 extends to 512-bit `zmm` registers (16 floats).

How does the x87 FPU work in x86-64 assembly?

The x87 FPU is the legacy floating-point unit — it uses a stack of 8 registers (`st0` through `st7`):

```nasm
fld     qword [val]       ; push val onto FP stack (st0 = val)
fld     qword [val2]      ; push val2 (st0=val2, st1=old val)
fadd                      ; st0 = st0 + st1 (pop both, push result)
fstp    qword [result]    ; pop st0 and store to memory

; Other FP operations
fmul    st0, st1          ; st0 = st0 * st1
fdiv    st0, st1          ; st0 = st0 / st1
fsqrt                     ; st0 = sqrt(st0)
fabs                      ; st0 = |st0|
fchs                      ; st0 = -st0  (change sign)
```

The x87 FPU is mostly legacy — prefer SSE2/AVX for new code. It is still used for **80-bit long double** (`long double` in C on Linux).

    msg db "Hello", 10    ; string + newline
    msglen equ $ - msg    ; length

global _start

    mov rdx, msglen       ; number of bytes

How do you use local labels inside NASM macros to avoid label conflicts?

```nasm
%macro print_newline 0
    push rax
    push rdi
    push rsi
    push rdx
    mov  rax, 1
    mov  rdi, 1
    mov  rsi, .nl        ; local label — unique per macro expansion
    mov  rdx, 1
    syscall
    pop  rdx
    pop  rsi
    pop  rdi
    pop  rax
    jmp  .end            ; jump past the data
.nl: db 10               ; newline byte embedded in code
.end:
%endmacro
```

Labels starting with `.` inside a macro are **local** — NASM generates a unique name for each macro expansion, so using the same macro multiple times does not cause duplicate label errors.

Why is XOR used to zero a register instead of MOV in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
xor rax, rax       ; rax = 0  (preferred)
mov rax, 0         ; rax = 0  (also works but less efficient)
```

`xor rax, rax` is preferred because:
1. **Smaller encoding** — `xor eax, eax` encodes in 2 bytes; `mov rax, 0` can be 5–10 bytes
2. **Dependency breaking** — the CPU recognizes `xor reg, reg` as independent of the previous value of `reg`, enabling better pipelining
3. **Zeroing the full 64-bit register** — writing to `eax` (32-bit) zero-extends to `rax`, so `xor eax, eax` is equivalent to `xor rax, rax`

This is one of the most common assembly micro-optimizations.

How does the stack work in x86-64? Which direction does it grow?

The stack grows **downward** — toward lower memory addresses.

```nasm
push rax        ; rsp -= 8, then memory[rsp] = rax
                ; (stack grows down by 8 bytes)

pop  rbx        ; rbx = memory[rsp], then rsp += 8
                ; (stack shrinks up by 8 bytes)
```

Visually:
```
High addresses
  [previous frame]
  [return address]  ← rsp after call
  [saved rbp]       ← rsp after push rbp
  [local variables] ← rsp after sub rsp, N
Low addresses
```

The stack must be **16-byte aligned** before any `call` instruction (System V ABI requirement). A misaligned stack can cause crashes with SSE instructions.

What is the difference between signed and unsigned jumps in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
; After: cmp rax, rbx

; Signed jumps (interpret values as two's complement signed integers)
jg  label  ; jump if rax > rbx  (signed greater)
jl  label  ; jump if rax < rbx  (signed less)
jge label  ; jump if rax >= rbx
jle label  ; jump if rax <= rbx

; Unsigned jumps (interpret values as unsigned integers)
ja  label  ; jump if rax > rbx  (unsigned above)
jb  label  ; jump if rax < rbx  (unsigned below)
jae label  ; jump if rax >= rbx
jbe label  ; jump if rax <= rbx
```

Example: `-1` as a 64-bit unsigned value is `0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` (very large).
- Signed: `-1 < 0` → `jl` would jump
- Unsigned: `0xFFFFFFFF... > 0` → `ja` would jump

Choose signed (`jg/jl`) for signed integers and unsigned (`ja/jb`) for pointers and unsigned values.

How do you implement an if-else in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
; C equivalent: if (rax > rbx) { rax = rax - rbx; } else { rax = rbx - rax; }

    cmp rax, rbx
    jle .else_branch        ; jump to else if NOT (rax > rbx)

.if_branch:
    sub rax, rbx
    jmp .end_if

.else_branch:
    sub rbx, rax
    mov rax, rbx

.end_if:
    ; continue
```

Alternatively using CMOV (branchless):
```nasm
    cmp  rax, rbx
    cmovle rax, rbx         ; if rax <= rbx: rax = rbx (no branch!)
```

Branchless code with `cmov` is often faster due to avoiding branch mispredictions.

What does 'global _start' mean in NASM and why is it needed?

    global _start    ; export _start symbol to the linker

_start:
    ; program entry point

What does the variadic function calling convention look like in x86-64 assembly?

```nasm
; Variadic function: print_ints(count, v1, v2, ...)
; rdi = count
; rsi = v1
; rdx = v2
; rcx = v3
; r8  = v4
; r9  = v5
; [rsp+8]  = v6  (first stack argument after return address)
; [rsp+16] = v7
; ...
print_ints:
    push rbp
    mov  rbp, rsp
    ; access stack args:
    mov  rax, [rbp + 16]   ; v6 (7th argument)
    mov  rax, [rbp + 24]   ; v7 (8th argument)
    pop  rbp
    ret
```

For `printf` and other C variadic functions, the number of XMM registers used must also be passed in `rax` before the call.
